transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Meridian Head of Platform), Priya Shah (Meridian ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Meridian SRE)

00:00 Sofia (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for making time, um quick round robin — i think we have about 50 minutes, is that still good?
00:04 Carlos (Meridian): yep that's perfect, we've blocked the hour. we'll start with our performance goals then dig into security.
00:09 Sofia: awesome. quick intro on our side, i'm sofia, AE at Redwood, and ethan's our solutions engineer who will run through the perf stuff.
00:15 Ethan (Redwood SE): hey all, hi there, i'll be the hands-on SE. i can go deep on batching, kv cache, and streaming behavior.
00:22 Priya (Meridian): i'm priya, i own model infra and the prompt library. we're trying to figure out whether hosted will work for us or we need dedicated or private given p95 and compliance.
00:29 Liam (Meridian): liam here, sre, mostly concerned with tail latency and operational fallback — we run route optimization queries with tight SLAs.
00:36 Sofia: great. starting with high-level goals — can you share the p95 SLA you're targeting and concurrency?
00:42 Carlos: sure. target p95 under 250ms for short prompts (avg 128 tokens), but we also have medium flows up to 4k tokens where p95 should be under 2s ideally. concurrency-wise we need to support 600 concurrent sessions at peak, and sustained throughput about 6k tokens/sec across the fleet.
01:00 Ethan: ok that's helpful. couple clarifying q's — when you say 600 concurrent sessions is that concurrent open streams or concurrent in-flight requests?
01:06 Carlos: mostly concurrent streaming sessions, many are websocket streams that expect token-by-token updates. some are fire-and-forget calls too.
01:14 Ethan: makes sense. so we need to plan for streaming-friendly serving with small token latency. on hosted we have streaming endpoints that maintain low tail latency but dedicated gives you more predictable throughput for sustained token/sec.
01:26 Priya: what does predictable mean — is it absolute or percent improvements? e.g., we saw spikes when batch sizes changed in our current infra.
01:33 Ethan: good q. predictable means we can promise reserved GPU pools, autoscale policies and a burst buffer. so for Dedicated you commit to capacity and we guarantee throughput bands; hosted is multi-tenant so you can see more variance during global load peaks but typically is fine for many customers.
01:46 Liam: and private would be on our VPC / on-prem? what are the main tradeoffs there?
01:50 Sofia: exactly. Private gives you full control of networking and KMS integration, and you host the runtime (or we deploy into your infra). it helps with data residency and strict audit requirements but adds ops overhead — we can still provide the control plane for rollouts if you want.
01:59 Carlos: ok. digging into measurement — how do you measure p95 for streaming? is it token-to-token, final token, or first-byte?
02:05 Ethan: streaming p95 is usually measured as first-byte latency for the first N tokens and then token step latency distribution for subsequent tokens; for your route optimization use-case I would recommend tracking both initial response p95 and steady-state token latency p95. e.g., first-token p95 under 250ms, subsequent token-step p95 under 50ms if you're doing small tokens, but that depends on model and batch policies.
02:26 Priya: what's the impact of batching on streaming latency?
02:29 Ethan: batching reduces per-token cost but can increase tail latency — continuous batching attempts to flush after a short delay while still aggregating requests. you can tune the max batch window or set latency SLOs which will force smaller batches. on Dedicated you can run bigger batch sizes without neighbor noise, so you trade cost for consistent latency.
02:43 Carlos: what about kv cache for our 4k sequences — can that avoid re-computation?
02:47 Ethan: yes, KV cache helps a lot for long contexts; we support efficient cache reuse across streaming sessions. for very long sequences you can checkpoint and reuse, but it will increase memory pressure; Dedicated can provide larger kv memory budgets per worker.
02:57 Liam: operationally, if there's a spike beyond our reserved capacity what happens? do you drop streams? degrade?
03:02 Sofia: we have multi-tier fallbacks: first, automatic model variants (smaller quantized models) to degrade gracefully; second, routing to another region or capacity tier; third, throttling policies per token or per-session. we'll work with you to define fallback priorities.
03:15 Carlos: interesting. example numbers — for a 4k seq with a 32k context model, what p95 should we expect on Dedicated vs Hosted?
03:22 Ethan: rough order: Dedicated with A100-class pools and optimized kernels, you can see p95s around 1.1–1.8s for a 4k generation depending on tokens generated. Hosted multi-tenant might be 1.5–2.5s under load. that's rough — we'll run benchmarks.
03:38 Priya: ok. can we run token/sec benchmarks that simulate bursty traffic and steady-state?
03:42 Ethan: yes, we usually run a few canonical bench types: burst ramp, steady-state sustained QPS, and streaming token-step latency traces. we'll simulate your prompt mix and sequence lengths.
03:52 Carlos: how do we ensure bench comparability — same hardware, same model weights?
03:55 Ethan: we'll pin the model revision id, quantization config, and provide the exact kernel/runtime flags. for Dedicated we can match hardware (we'll provision similar GPUs) but Hosted runs on our fleet; results will include hardware metadata.
04:07 Liam: any gotchas on your end — warm vs cold caches? we need realistic coldstart behavior included.
04:11 Ethan: good call — benches will include cold-start runs and warmed runs; we'll also test KV cache hit ratios and multi-tenant noise scenarios.
04:19 Priya: about measurement granularity, can you emit per-token latency traces?
04:22 Ethan: yes we can capture per-token timing and export as CSV or jsonl so you can compute percentiles. our console can chart per-route token step p95.
04:31 Carlos: on security, we need SSO, SAML, audit logs, and HSM integration for keys. support for customer-managed KMS is required.
04:38 Sofia: we support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private/Dedicated. Hosted also supports BYOK via KMS in supported regions — we'll send the whitepaper.
04:46 Liam: any SOC
04:47 Speaker 2: two, yes we are SOC 2 Type II.
04:49 Sofia: (laughs) yes, sorry, we are SOC 2 Type II and we have ISO certs for certain regions, will include compliance packet.
04:55 Carlos: competitor question — we've been talking to Replicate and CloudX for similar infra. how do you compare on throughput?
04:59 Ethan: Replicate tends to be more self-serve but less focused on dedicated reserved guarantees; CloudX offers dedicated but we differentiate with unified runtime and smarter kernel selection and routing policies that optimize latency/cost tradeoffs.
05:12 Priya: ok pricing shape — for Dedicated, do you charge per-GPU + token overages?
05:16 Sofia: Dedicated is reserved capacity (monthly commit) with a base rate per GPU class and committed token throughput; overages billed at unit rates. we can show an example term sheet after we define the sizing.
05:25 Carlos: for our internal buy-in we need a clear expected unit cost at target throughput — can you model cost per 1k tokens at 6k token/sec sustained?
05:33 Ethan: we can model that; we'll produce a unit economics spreadsheet showing per-token cost under different batching and quantization profiles.
05:41 Priya: streaming engineering detail — websocket disconnects mid-stream, is there automatic resume or do we need to handle replays?
05:47 Ethan: currently client should handle reconnect and state management; for Private we can add sticky session support and for Dedicated we offer better session affinity. we also support checkpointed KV states to resume efficiently.
05:58 Liam: curious about quantization: will int8 affect token-step latency?
06:02 Ethan: quantization helps reduce memory and can speed throughput on some kernels, but may increase single-token latency slightly depending on kernels; we recommend benchmark to see tradeoffs for your model.
06:11 Carlos: let's talk concrete bench plan — what's the minimum we need to provide?
06:14 Ethan: we need your canonical prompt set (representative frequency by token length), desired sequence outputs, and expected concurrency profile (burst patterns). we'll run 3 runs: cold-start ramp, steady-state 30-minute run, and burst storm. we'll capture per-token p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and tail latency.
06:33 Priya: sounds good. can you simulate our real-time routing (we have region-aware endpoints)?
06:37 Ethan: yes, we can run region-to-region routing in bench harness. note that cross-region adds network latency; we'll include a regional baseline.
06:45 Sofia: quick recap — Redwood to run benchmarks for Hosted and Dedicated variants, include streaming and non-streaming traces, produce unit-cost model, and share security packet. Meridian to send canonical prompts and p95 targets.
06:58 Carlos: yep and we'll try to get legal/ops to sign off on the data-share for benching — may need an MSA addendum.
07:05 Sofia: understood. one more question from liam — how do rollouts and canaries affect latency during upgrade?
07:11 Ethan: rollouts use canary traffic slices; the runtime can route a small % to new model or kernel; we monitor p95 and auto-rollback if we see regressions. it adds minimal extra latency because most traffic hits the baseline pool until cutover.
07:22 Priya: last q — if we want Private on-prem later, how hard is migration?
07:26 Sofia: we design configs to be portable; model artifacts, quantization profiles, and rollout configs can be exported. Private migration requires network config and an ops window, but we've done several migrations with predictable timelines.
07:36 Carlos: ok perfect. let's confirm the dates — sofia you said security docs by tomorrow?
07:40 Sofia: yes i'll share by 2026-08-06, and ethan will push the bench plan by EOD 2026-08-06.
07:45 Carlos: great. thanks everyone.
07:47 Sofia: thanks for the time, we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule the bench review for the 12th.
07:52 (call ends)
